statement: Every square matrix $A$ over a [field](c:field) factors as $PA = LU$, where $P$ is a [permutation matrix](c:permutation-matrix), $L$ is [lower triangular](c:lower-triangular-matrix) with ones on the diagonal and $U$ is [upper triangular](c:upper-triangular-matrix). If the leading principal minors of orders $1, \dots, n-1$ are nonzero, $P = I$ works.

hypotheses.text: The matrix $A$ is an $n \times n$ matrix over a [field](c:field) $K$.
For the case $P = I$: the leading principal minors $\Delta_1, \dots, \Delta_{n-1}$ of $A$ are nonzero.

conclusion: There are $P$, $L$ and $U$ as stated with $PA = LU$, and $P = I$ when the leading minors $\Delta_1, \dots, \Delta_{n-1}$ are nonzero.

proofs.name: Gaussian elimination with row swaps
proofs.slogan: Elimination with row swaps turns $A$ into $U$ by unit lower [triangular](c:triangular-matrix) steps, and collecting the steps gives $L$ and $P$.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem for $n \ge 1$; a column with no nonzero entry on or below the diagonal needs no elimination, and its swap is the identity. Step 5 treats the case of nonzero leading minors.

roles.why: Division by a nonzero pivot needs a [field](c:field), and the square shape makes $U$ square.
Nonzero leading minors make every pivot nonzero, so no swap is needed.

steps.slogan: Swap a nonzero pivot into row $k$ and clear the entries below it.
steps.detail: At stage $k$, a transposition matrix $P_k$ moves a row $i \ge k$ with nonzero entry in column $k$ to row $k$ ($P_k = I$ if there is none). Subtracting $\ell_{ik} = a_{ik}/a_{kk}$ times row $k$ from each row $i > k$ is multiplication by $M_k = I - \ell_k e_k^{T}$, a unit [lower triangular matrix](c:lower-triangular-matrix).

steps.slogan: Repeat the stage for each column to reach an upper triangular matrix.
steps.detail: After stages $k = 1, \dots, n-1$, the matrix $U = M_{n-1}P_{n-1} \cdots M_1 P_1 A$ has zeros below the diagonal, so it is [upper triangular](c:upper-triangular-matrix). Each stage combines only rows $k, \dots, n$, so it keeps the zeros of earlier columns.

steps.slogan: Move every row swap to the right of the elimination matrices.
steps.detail: For $j > k$ the swap $P_j$ exchanges two rows with index greater than $k$, so $P_j M_k = \tilde M_k P_j$ with $\tilde M_k$ equal to $M_k$ with permuted multipliers, still unit lower triangular. Hence $\tilde M_{n-1} \cdots \tilde M_1 P A = U$ with the [permutation matrix](c:permutation-matrix) $P = P_{n-1} \cdots P_1$.

steps.slogan: Show that nonzero leading minors give nonzero pivots without any swap.
steps.detail: Without swaps, stage $k$ adds multiples of row $k$ to later rows, so it keeps every leading principal minor. After $k-1$ stages the leading $k \times k$ block is upper triangular, so $\Delta_k = u_{11} \cdots u_{kk}$ by the [determinant](c:determinant) of a triangular block, and $u_{kk} = \Delta_k / \Delta_{k-1} \ne 0$ for $k < n$. So every $P_k = I$.

steps.slogan: Invert the product of unit lower triangular matrices to obtain $L$.
steps.detail: Products and inverses of unit lower triangular matrices are unit lower triangular, with $\tilde M_k^{-1} = I + \tilde\ell_k e_k^{T}$. So $L = (\tilde M_{n-1} \cdots \tilde M_1)^{-1}$ is unit lower triangular and $PA = LU$, with $P = I$ in the case of step 4.

concepts.c:field: Pivots must be invertible scalars, so the entries lie in a field.
concepts.c:permutation-matrix: The row swaps collect into one permutation matrix $P$.
concepts.c:lower-triangular-matrix: Each elimination step and the factor $L$ are unit lower triangular.
concepts.c:upper-triangular-matrix: Elimination ends at the upper triangular factor $U$.
concepts.c:triangular-matrix: Triangular matrices are closed under products and inverses here.
concepts.c:determinant: Leading minors are determinants that equal products of pivots.

source.note: Gaussian elimination with partial pivoting, as in G. H. Golub and C. F. Van Loan, Matrix Computations, chapter 3.

statement: Let $(\mathcal F_n)$ be a [filtration](c:filtration) on a finite measure space $(\Omega, \mathcal F, \mu)$, let $g$ be an [integrable function](c:integrable-function) and let $\mathcal F_\infty = \bigvee_n \mathcal F_n$. Then the [conditional expectations](c:conditional-expectation) $E[g \mid \mathcal F_n]$ converge to $E[g \mid \mathcal F_\infty]$ in $L^1$ and [almost everywhere](c:almost-everywhere).

hypotheses.text: The measure $\mu$ is finite.
The $\sigma$-algebras $\mathcal F_n \subseteq \mathcal F$ increase with $n$ and form a [filtration](c:filtration).
The function $g$ is [integrable](c:integrable-function).

conclusion: $\|E[g \mid \mathcal F_n] - E[g \mid \mathcal F_\infty]\|_1 \to 0$ and $E[g \mid \mathcal F_n] \to E[g \mid \mathcal F_\infty]$ almost everywhere.

formal.difference: The declaration gives the $L^1$ convergence only; the almost everywhere convergence is MeasureTheory.tendsto_ae_condExp. It has no integrability hypothesis, because mathlib sets the conditional expectation of a non-integrable function to $0$.

proofs.name: Tower property, martingale limit and Vitali
proofs.slogan: Replace $g$ by $h = E[g \mid \mathcal F_\infty]$, let the martingale $E[h \mid \mathcal F_n]$ converge, upgrade by uniform integrability and identify the limit with $h$.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem for real-valued $g$. If $\mu = 0$, every statement is trivial.

roles.why: A finite measure lets the martingale convergence theorem apply and makes almost everywhere convergence imply convergence in measure.
Increasing $\sigma$-algebras give the tower property, make $(M_n)$ a martingale and make $\bigcup_n \mathcal F_n$ a π-system.
Integrability of $g$ makes $h$ integrable and bounds the martingale in $L^1$.

steps.slogan: Replace $g$ by $h = E[g \mid \mathcal F_\infty]$ through the tower property.
steps.detail: Since $\mathcal F_n \subseteq \mathcal F_\infty$, the tower property gives $E[h \mid \mathcal F_n] = E[g \mid \mathcal F_n]$ almost everywhere for every $n$. So it suffices to prove $M_n = E[h \mid \mathcal F_n] \to h$ for the $\mathcal F_\infty$-measurable [integrable function](c:integrable-function) $h$.

steps.slogan: Show that the [martingale](c:martingale) $M_n$ is bounded in $L^1$ and uniformly integrable.
steps.detail: Conditional Jensen gives $|M_n| \le E[|h| \mid \mathcal F_n]$, so $\|M_n\|_1 \le \|h\|_1$, $\mu(|M_n| > K) \le \|h\|_1 / K$ and $\int_{\{|M_n| > K\}} |M_n| \le \int_{\{|M_n| > K\}} |h|$. Absolute continuity of the integral of $|h|$ makes this small uniformly in $n$, which is [uniform integrability](c:uniform-integrability).

steps.slogan: Let the $L^1$-bounded martingale converge almost everywhere to a limit $M_\infty$.
steps.detail: The almost everywhere martingale convergence theorem gives an $\mathcal F_\infty$-measurable $M_\infty$ with $M_n \to M_\infty$ [almost everywhere](c:almost-everywhere). Fatou's lemma and the bound $\|M_n\|_1 \le \|h\|_1$ make $M_\infty$ integrable.

steps.slogan: Upgrade the almost everywhere convergence to $L^1$ convergence by Vitali's theorem.
steps.detail: On a finite measure space, almost everywhere convergence implies [convergence in measure](c:convergence-in-measure). With uniform integrability, the Vitali convergence theorem gives $\|M_n - M_\infty\|_1 \to 0$.

steps.slogan: Identify $M_\infty$ with $h$ by integrals over the sets of $\bigcup_n \mathcal F_n$.
steps.detail: For $A \in \mathcal F_m$ and $n \ge m$, $\int_A M_n = \int_A h$, and the $L^1$ limit gives $\int_A M_\infty = \int_A h$. These sets form a [π-system](c:pi-system) that generates $\mathcal F_\infty$, so Dynkin's theorem extends the equality to $\mathcal F_\infty$ and $M_\infty = h$ almost everywhere. Hence $E[g \mid \mathcal F_n] = M_n \to h$ almost everywhere and in $L^1$.

concepts.c:filtration: The increasing sigma-algebras define the martingale and its limit sigma-algebra.
concepts.c:integrable-function: Integrability of $g$ gives an integrable $h$ and an $L^1$ bound.
concepts.c:conditional-expectation: The theorem is about limits of conditional expectations of one function.
concepts.c:almost-everywhere: The martingale limit exists outside a null set.
concepts.c:martingale: The sequence $E[h \mid \mathcal F_n]$ is a martingale, so it converges.
concepts.c:uniform-integrability: Uniform integrability turns almost everywhere convergence into $L^1$ convergence.
concepts.c:convergence-in-measure: Vitali's theorem needs convergence in measure, which a.e. convergence gives.
concepts.c:pi-system: Equality of integrals on a generating π-system extends to the sigma-algebra.

statement: Let $U \subseteq \mathbb{C}$ be an [open set](c:open-set) and $f\colon U \to \mathbb{C}$ a [holomorphic function](c:holomorphic-function). If $|f|$ has a local maximum at $c \in U$, then $f$ is constant on a neighborhood of $c$.

hypotheses.text: The function $f$ is [holomorphic](c:holomorphic-function) on the [open set](c:open-set) $U$.
The [modulus](c:norm) $|f|$ has a local maximum at $c \in U$: $|f(z)| \le |f(c)|$ for all $z$ near $c$.

conclusion: There is $r > 0$ with $f(z) = f(c)$ for all $z$ with $|z - c| \le r$.

formal.difference: The declaration is more general: $f\colon E \to F$ maps between complex normed spaces with $F$ strictly convex, and $f$ need only be differentiable near $c$. Constancy on a connected domain is the separate declaration Complex.eqOn_of_isPreconnected_of_isMaxOn_norm.

proofs.name: Cauchy formula on circles and strict convexity
proofs.slogan: The Cauchy integral formula makes $f(c)$ an average over circles, so $|f|$ is constant near $c$, and the function $f + f(c)$ then forces $f$ to be constant.
proofs.scope: The local statement; for a connected $U$ the identity theorem then gives constancy on all of $U$. The point $w = c$ needs no argument.

roles.why: Holomorphy on a disc in the open set gives the Cauchy integral formula and continuity of $f$.
The local maximum gives $|f| \le |f(c)|$ on a disc, the bound that the circle average must meet with equality.

steps.slogan: Choose a closed disc around $c$ on which $f$ is holomorphic and $|f| \le |f(c)|$.
steps.detail: Since $U$ is open and $|f|$ has a local maximum at $c$, there is $r > 0$ with $\overline{D}(c, r) \subseteq U$ and $|f(z)| \le |f(c)|$ on $\overline{D}(c, r)$. Both properties hold on every smaller concentric disc.

steps.slogan: Write $f(c)$ as the average of $f$ over the circle through a point $w$.
steps.detail: For $w \ne c$ in the disc and $\rho = |w - c|$, the Cauchy integral formula gives $f(c) = \frac{1}{2\pi} \int_0^{2\pi} f(c + \rho e^{i\theta}) \, d\theta$.

steps.slogan: Show that $|f(w)| = |f(c)|$ by a strict estimate of the circle average.
steps.detail: If $|f(w)| < |f(c)|$, continuity gives $|f| < |f(c)|$ on an arc of the circle, and $|f| \le |f(c)|$ on the rest. Then $|f(c)| \le \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi} |f(c + \rho e^{i\theta})| \, d\theta < |f(c)|$, a contradiction. So $|f| = |f(c)|$ on the disc.

steps.slogan: Apply steps 2 and 3 to $f + f(c)$ to get $|f(w) + f(c)| = 2|f(c)|$.
steps.detail: The function $f + f(c)$ is holomorphic, and $|f(z) + f(c)| \le |f(z)| + |f(c)| \le 2|f(c)|$ on the disc, with equality at $z = c$. So its modulus also has a maximum at $c$, and steps 2 and 3 give $|f(w) + f(c)| = 2|f(c)|$.

steps.slogan: Use equality in the triangle inequality to conclude $f(w) = f(c)$.
steps.detail: Now $|f(w)| = |f(c)|$ and $|f(w) + f(c)| = |f(w)| + |f(c)|$. Because $\mathbb{C}$ is a [strictly convex space](c:strict-convex-space), equality in the triangle inequality puts $f(w)$ and $f(c)$ on one ray from $0$, and equal moduli give $f(w) = f(c)$.

concepts.c:open-set: Openness of $U$ gives a closed disc around $c$ inside $U$.
concepts.c:holomorphic-function: Holomorphy gives the Cauchy integral formula on every circle in the disc.
concepts.c:norm: The hypothesis bounds the modulus, and the proof compares moduli of averages.
concepts.c:strict-convex-space: Strict convexity of $\mathbb{C}$ turns equal norms into equal values.

proofs.name: Power series and Parseval
proofs.slogan: Expand $f$ in a power series at $c$ and compare the mean of $|f|^2$ on a circle with $|f(c)|^2$.
proofs.scope: The local statement on a disc of convergence inside $U$ on which $|f| \le |f(c)|$.

roles.why: Holomorphy on the open set gives a convergent power series on a disc around $c$.
The local maximum bounds the circle mean of $|f|^2$ by $|f(c)|^2$.

steps.slogan: Expand $f$ as a power series on a disc around $c$.
steps.detail: A [holomorphic function](c:holomorphic-function) on the [open set](c:open-set) $U$ is analytic, so $f(z) = \sum_{n \ge 0} a_n (z - c)^n$ on a disc $|z - c| < R$ inside $U$, with $a_0 = f(c)$. Shrink $R$ so that $|f| \le |f(c)|$ on this disc.

steps.slogan: Compute the mean of $|f|^2$ on a circle by orthogonality of the exponentials $e^{in\theta}$.
steps.detail: For $0 < \rho < R$ the series converges uniformly on $|z - c| = \rho$, and $\int_0^{2\pi} e^{i(n-m)\theta}\,d\theta = 0$ for $n \ne m$. Hence $\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi} |f(c + \rho e^{i\theta})|^2 \, d\theta = \sum_{n \ge 0} |a_n|^2 \rho^{2n}$.

steps.slogan: Bound the mean by $|f(c)|^2$ and deduce that all higher coefficients vanish.
steps.detail: The bound $|f| \le |f(c)|$ makes the mean at most $|f(c)|^2 = |a_0|^2$, so $\sum_{n \ge 1} |a_n|^2 \rho^{2n} \le 0$. Hence $a_n = 0$ for $n \ge 1$, and $f = a_0 = f(c)$ on the disc.

concepts.c:open-set: Openness of $U$ leaves room for a disc of convergence around $c$.
concepts.c:holomorphic-function: Holomorphic functions have convergent power series, the object of this proof.
concepts.c:norm: The modulus bound controls the mean square of $f$ on circles.

source.note: The classical Gutzmer-Parseval argument for power series; not the mathlib route.

statement: Let $(X, \mu)$ be a measure space, $1 \le p < \infty$ and $f, g \in L^p(\mu)$. Then $f + g \in L^p(\mu)$ and $\|f + g\|_p \le \|f\|_p + \|g\|_p$, so the $p$-[norm](c:norm) satisfies the triangle inequality on the [Lp space](c:lp-space).

hypotheses.text: The exponent satisfies $1 \le p < \infty$.
The functions $f$ and $g$ lie in the [Lp space](c:lp-space): they are measurable with $\int |f|^p \, d\mu < \infty$ and $\int |g|^p \, d\mu < \infty$.

formal.difference: The declaration treats nonnegative families $f, g\colon \iota \to [0, \infty)$ with summable $p$-th powers, which is the counting measure case. It also states that $(f_i + g_i)^p$ is summable.

proofs.name: Hölder duality
proofs.slogan: Test $|f| + |g|$ against the Hölder-extremal function of unit $q$-norm and split the pairing into two Hölder bounds.
proofs.scope: The case $p = 1$ follows from $|f + g| \le |f| + |g|$ by integration, so the steps treat $1 < p < \infty$. The case $\||f| + |g|\|_p = 0$ is trivial.

roles.why: The bound $p \ge 1$ makes $t \mapsto t^p$ convex and gives the conjugate exponent $q = p/(p-1)$.
Finite $p$-norms of $f$ and $g$ make $\||f| + |g|\|_p$ finite, so the extremal function is defined.

steps.slogan: Bound $(|f| + |g|)^p$ by convexity of $t \mapsto t^p$ to stay in $L^p$.
steps.detail: [Convexity](c:convex-function) of $t^p$ on $[0, \infty)$ gives $\left(\frac{a + b}{2}\right)^p \le \frac{a^p + b^p}{2}$, so $(|f| + |g|)^p \le 2^{p-1}(|f|^p + |g|^p)$. Integration gives $\|h\|_p < \infty$ for $h = |f| + |g|$, and $|f + g| \le h$.

steps.slogan: Apply Hölder's inequality with the conjugate exponent $q = p/(p-1)$.
steps.detail: For measurable $\varphi \ge 0$ with $\|\varphi\|_q \le 1$, Hölder's inequality gives $\int |f| \varphi \, d\mu \le \|f\|_p \|\varphi\|_q \le \|f\|_p$, and in the same way $\int |g| \varphi \, d\mu \le \|g\|_p$.

steps.slogan: Choose $\varphi = h^{p-1} / \|h\|_p^{p-1}$, the function that attains the duality bound for $h$.
steps.detail: If $0 < \|h\|_p < \infty$, then $\varphi^q = h^p / \|h\|_p^p$ because $(p-1)q = p$, so $\|\varphi\|_q = 1$. Also $\int h \varphi \, d\mu = \|h\|_p^p / \|h\|_p^{p-1} = \|h\|_p$.

steps.slogan: Split the pairing of $h$ with $\varphi$ into the two Hölder bounds.
steps.detail: By steps 2 and 3, $\|f + g\|_p \le \|h\|_p = \int |f| \varphi \, d\mu + \int |g| \varphi \, d\mu \le \|f\|_p + \|g\|_p$. This is the triangle inequality for the $p$-[norm](c:norm).

concepts.c:norm: The inequality is the triangle inequality of the $p$-norm.
concepts.c:lp-space: Membership in $L^p$ makes all norms in the argument finite.
concepts.c:convex-function: Convexity of $t^p$ shows that $|f| + |g|$ stays in $L^p$.

source.note: mathlib proves the finite-sum case NNReal.Lp_add_le by the same duality (isGreatest_Lp, from Hölder inner_le_Lp_mul_Lq) and passes to infinite sums by bounding partial sums; the steps run the duality for a general measure.

proofs.name: Convexity of the unit ball
proofs.slogan: Normalize $f$ and $g$ to unit norm and use convexity of $t \mapsto t^p$ to keep their weighted average in the unit ball.
proofs.scope: All $1 \le p < \infty$. If $\|f\|_p = 0$ or $\|g\|_p = 0$, that function vanishes almost everywhere and the inequality is an equality.

roles.why: For $p \ge 1$ the map $t \mapsto t^p$ is convex on $[0, \infty)$.
Finite norms $a$ and $b$ allow the normalization.

steps.slogan: Set $a = \|f\|_p$ and $b = \|g\|_p$ and normalize the two functions.
steps.detail: Assume $a, b > 0$ and put $u = |f|/a$ and $v = |g|/b$, so $\int u^p \, d\mu = \int v^p \, d\mu = 1$. With $\lambda = a/(a+b) \in (0, 1)$, we get $\frac{|f| + |g|}{a + b} = \lambda u + (1 - \lambda) v$.

steps.slogan: Bound the $p$-th power of the average by the average of the $p$-th powers.
steps.detail: [Convexity](c:convex-function) of $t \mapsto t^p$ on $[0, \infty)$ for $p \ge 1$ gives $(\lambda u + (1-\lambda) v)^p \le \lambda u^p + (1 - \lambda) v^p$ at every point.

steps.slogan: Integrate the pointwise bound and undo the normalization.
steps.detail: Integration gives $\int \left(\frac{|f| + |g|}{a + b}\right)^p d\mu \le \lambda + (1 - \lambda) = 1$. Hence $\|f + g\|_p \le \||f| + |g|\|_p \le a + b$, which is finite, so $f + g$ lies in the [Lp space](c:lp-space).

concepts.c:norm: The proof shows that the unit ball of the $p$-norm is convex.
concepts.c:lp-space: Normalization uses the finite $L^p$ norms of $f$ and $g$.
concepts.c:convex-function: Convexity of $t^p$ is the only inequality the proof needs.

source.note: The standard convexity proof: the unit ball of $L^p$ is convex because $t \mapsto t^p$ is convex; not the mathlib route.

statement: Let $A$ be an [abelian variety](c:abelian-variety) over a [number field](c:number-field) $K$. Then the group $A(K)$ of $K$-[rational points](c:rational-point) of $A$ is a [finitely generated](c:finitely-generated-group) [abelian group](c:abelian-group).

hypotheses.text: The variety $A$ is an [abelian variety](c:abelian-variety) defined over $K$.
The field $K$ is a [number field](c:number-field), a finite extension of $\mathbb{Q}$.

conclusion: $A(K) \cong \mathbb{Z}^r \oplus T$ for some rank $r \ge 0$ and some finite group $T$.

proofs.name: Weak Mordell–Weil theorem and height descent
proofs.slogan: Show that $A(K)/mA(K)$ is finite, then use a canonical height to descend from any point to finitely many points of small height.
proofs.scope: An outline of the published proof; steps 1 and 2 rest on the cited work. The case of an [elliptic curve](c:elliptic-curve) over $\mathbb{Q}$ is Mordell's theorem of 1922.

roles.why: The group law and a symmetric ample divisor on $A$ give the Kummer map and the quadratic canonical height.
Over a number field the class group is finite, the unit groups are finitely generated and Northcott's finiteness holds.

steps.slogan: Prove the weak Mordell–Weil theorem: $A(K)/mA(K)$ is finite for an integer $m \ge 2$.
steps.detail: Over a finite extension $L$ of $K$ that contains the points of $A[m]$, the Kummer map embeds $A(L)/mA(L)$ into homomorphisms $\mathrm{Gal}(\bar K/L) \to A[m]$ unramified outside a finite set $S$ of primes. Finiteness of the [ideal class group](c:ideal-class-group) and finite generation of the $S$-units bound these, and the kernel of $A(K)/mA(K) \to A(L)/mA(L)$ is finite by Galois cohomology.

steps.slogan: Construct the canonical height $\hat h$ on $A(K)$ from a symmetric ample divisor.
steps.detail: A [height function](c:height-function) $h$ from a symmetric ample divisor satisfies $h(2P) = 4h(P) + O(1)$. The Néron–Tate limit $\hat h(P) = \lim_n 4^{-n} h(2^n P)$ is a nonnegative quadratic form on $A(K)$ with $\hat h = h + O(1)$.

steps.slogan: Show that only finitely many points of $A(K)$ have bounded canonical height.
steps.detail: Since $\hat h = h + O(1)$, a bound on $\hat h$ bounds the Weil height of the projective coordinates of the point. Northcott's theorem gives only finitely many points of $\mathbb{P}^N(K)$ of bounded height.

steps.slogan: Descend from any point to points of small height and conclude finite generation.
steps.detail: Let $Q_1, \dots, Q_s$ represent $A(K)/mA(K)$ and $c = \max_i \sqrt{\hat h(Q_i)}$. Writing $P = mP_1 + Q_i$, the seminorm $\sqrt{\hat h}$ gives $\sqrt{\hat h(P_1)} \le (\sqrt{\hat h(P)} + c)/m$, which is smaller than $\sqrt{\hat h(P)}$ when that exceeds $c$. So the finitely many points with $\sqrt{\hat h} \le c$ and the $Q_i$ generate $A(K)$, and the structure theorem gives $\mathbb{Z}^r \oplus T$.

concepts.c:abelian-variety: The group structure of the abelian variety drives both the Kummer map and the height.
concepts.c:number-field: Arithmetic finiteness over number fields makes the weak theorem and Northcott work.
concepts.c:rational-point: The theorem describes the group of points with coordinates in $K$.
concepts.c:finitely-generated-group: Finite generation is what the descent proves.
concepts.c:abelian-group: The rational points form an abelian group under the group law.
concepts.c:elliptic-curve: Elliptic curves are the one-dimensional case, Mordell's original theorem.
concepts.c:height-function: Heights measure arithmetic size, and the descent makes them decrease.
concepts.c:ideal-class-group: Finiteness of the class group bounds the Kummer extensions.

source.ref: M. Hindry and J. H. Silverman, Diophantine Geometry: An Introduction, Graduate Texts in Mathematics 201, Springer, 2000, Part C
source.note: Part C proves the weak Mordell–Weil theorem and the descent with the canonical heights of Part B; the theorem is due to L. J. Mordell (1922) for elliptic curves over $\mathbb{Q}$ and A. Weil (1929).

statement: Let $n \ge 2$ identical particles of half-integer spin have the one-particle [Hilbert space](c:hilbert-space) $\mathcal H$. If two of the one-particle states $\psi_1, \dots, \psi_n \in \mathcal H$ are equal, then the [antisymmetric](c:antisymmetric-wave-function) $n$-particle state $\psi_1 \wedge \dots \wedge \psi_n$ is zero, so no two such particles occupy the same one-particle state.

hypotheses.text: The particles are identical and have half-integer spin.
Two of the one-particle states coincide: $\psi_i = \psi_j$ for some $i \ne j$.

conclusion: $\psi_1 \wedge \dots \wedge \psi_n = 0$, so this configuration gives no normalizable state.

proofs.name: Sign of a transposition
proofs.slogan: A transposition fixes the product state but changes the sign of the antisymmetrizer, so the antisymmetrized state equals its own negative.
proofs.scope: The step from half-integer spin to antisymmetry is the spin-statistics theorem, which the proof cites. The rest is linear algebra in $\mathcal H^{\otimes n}$.

roles.why: Half-integer spin makes the particles fermions, so their joint states are antisymmetric.
Equal states make the product vector invariant under the transposition of the two places.

steps.slogan: Place the joint state in the antisymmetric subspace by the spin-statistics theorem.
steps.detail: The spin-statistics theorem makes particles of half-integer spin fermions, so their states lie in the range of $\mathcal A = \frac{1}{n!}\sum_{\sigma \in S_n} \operatorname{sgn}(\sigma) P_\sigma$ on the [tensor product](c:tensor-product) $\mathcal H^{\otimes n}$, where $P_\sigma$ permutes the factors. The state with one-particle states $\psi_k$ is $\psi_1 \wedge \dots \wedge \psi_n = \mathcal A \Psi$ with $\Psi = \psi_1 \otimes \dots \otimes \psi_n$.

steps.slogan: Show that the transposition $\tau = (i\,j)$ fixes the product vector $\Psi$.
steps.detail: The operator $P_\tau$ exchanges the factors in places $i$ and $j$ of $\Psi = \psi_1 \otimes \dots \otimes \psi_n$. Since $\psi_i = \psi_j$, the exchange returns the same vector, so $P_\tau \Psi = \Psi$.

steps.slogan: Compute $\mathcal A P_\tau = -\mathcal A$ from the [sign](c:signature-of-a-permutation) of a transposition.
steps.detail: Since $P_\sigma P_\tau = P_{\sigma\tau}$, the substitution $\rho = \sigma\tau$ gives $\mathcal A P_\tau = \frac{1}{n!}\sum_\rho \operatorname{sgn}(\rho\tau^{-1}) P_\rho = \operatorname{sgn}(\tau)\,\mathcal A$. A transposition has sign $-1$.

steps.slogan: Conclude that the antisymmetrized state equals its negative and therefore vanishes.
steps.detail: By steps 2 and 3, $\mathcal A \Psi = \mathcal A P_\tau \Psi = -\mathcal A \Psi$, so $2\mathcal A\Psi = 0$ and $\mathcal A \Psi = 0$ in the complex vector space. A zero vector has norm $0$ and is no [quantum state](c:quantum-state), so the two particles cannot share the state $\psi_i$.

concepts.c:hilbert-space: One-particle states are vectors of the Hilbert space $\mathcal H$.
concepts.c:antisymmetric-wave-function: Fermion states are antisymmetric, and antisymmetry forces the vanishing.
concepts.c:tensor-product: Joint states of $n$ particles live in the tensor power $\mathcal H^{\otimes n}$.
concepts.c:signature-of-a-permutation: The sign $-1$ of a transposition makes the state its own negative.
concepts.c:quantum-state: A physical state needs a nonzero vector, which the zero vector is not.

source.note: The standard argument, as in D. J. Griffiths, Introduction to Quantum Mechanics, section 5.1, with the spin-statistics theorem as the physical input.

statement: Let $\pi(x)$ be the number of [primes](c:prime-number) $p \le x$. Then $\pi(x)$ is [asymptotic](c:asymptotic) to $x / \log x$ as $x \to \infty$, where $\log$ is the natural [logarithm](c:logarithm): $\pi(x) \log x / x \to 1$.

proofs.name: Newman's analytic proof
proofs.slogan: Show that the [Riemann zeta function](c:riemann-zeta-function) has no zeros on $\operatorname{Re} s = 1$, feed this into Newman's Tauberian theorem for Laplace transforms, and deduce $\theta(x) \sim x$.
proofs.scope: An outline of Newman's proof in Zagier's account; the analytic theorem of step 4 rests on a contour integral of the cited paper. The proof works with $\theta(x) = \sum_{p \le x} \log p$ and $\Phi(s) = \sum_p \log p \; p^{-s}$.

steps.slogan: Bound the [Chebyshev function](c:chebyshev-function) $\theta(x)$ by $O(x)$ through the central binomial coefficient.
steps.detail: Every prime $p$ with $n < p \le 2n$ divides $\binom{2n}{n} \le 4^n$, so $\theta(2n) - \theta(n) \le 2n \log 2$. Summing this bound over $x, x/2, x/4, \dots$ gives $\theta(x) = O(x)$.

steps.slogan: Continue $\zeta(s) - \frac{1}{s-1}$ to $\operatorname{Re} s > 0$ and show $\zeta(s) \ne 0$ on $\operatorname{Re} s = 1$.
steps.detail: The Euler product gives $\zeta(s) \ne 0$ for $\operatorname{Re} s > 1$, and $\zeta(s) - \frac{1}{s-1} = \sum_n \int_n^{n+1} (n^{-s} - x^{-s}) \, dx$ is holomorphic for $\operatorname{Re} s > 0$. A zero at $1 + i\alpha$ would make $\sum_{r=-2}^{2} \binom{4}{2+r} \Phi(1 + \varepsilon + ir\alpha) = \sum_p \frac{\log p}{p^{1+\varepsilon}} (p^{i\alpha/2} + p^{-i\alpha/2})^4 \ge 0$ tend to $-\infty$ as $\varepsilon \to 0^+$.

steps.slogan: Show that $\Phi(s) - \frac{1}{s-1}$ extends holomorphically to $\operatorname{Re} s \ge 1$.
steps.detail: The logarithmic derivative of the Euler product gives $-\zeta'(s)/\zeta(s) = \Phi(s) + \sum_p \frac{\log p}{p^s(p^s - 1)}$, and the last sum is holomorphic for $\operatorname{Re} s > 1/2$. Since $\zeta$ has a simple pole at $1$ and no zeros on $\operatorname{Re} s \ge 1$, $\Phi(s) - \frac{1}{s-1}$ is holomorphic there.

steps.slogan: Prove Newman's analytic theorem for Laplace transforms by a contour integral.
steps.detail: Let $f$ be bounded and locally integrable on $[0, \infty)$, and let its [Laplace transform](c:laplace-transform) $g(z) = \int_0^\infty f(t) e^{-zt} \, dt$ extend holomorphically to $\operatorname{Re} z \ge 0$. The Cauchy integral formula for $g(z) e^{zT}(1 + z^2/R^2)/z$ on a contour bulging left of the imaginary axis shows $\int_0^T f(t) \, dt \to g(0)$ as $T \to \infty$.

steps.slogan: Apply the analytic theorem to $f(t) = \theta(e^t) e^{-t} - 1$.
steps.detail: Step 1 makes $f$ bounded, and $\int_0^\infty f(t) e^{-zt}\,dt = \frac{\Phi(z+1)}{z+1} - \frac{1}{z}$ is holomorphic on $\operatorname{Re} z \ge 0$ by step 3. Hence $\int_1^\infty \frac{\theta(x) - x}{x^2}\,dx$ converges.

steps.slogan: Deduce $\theta(x) \sim x$ from the convergent integral, and then $\pi(x) \sim x/\log x$.
steps.detail: If $\theta(x) \ge \lambda x$ with $\lambda > 1$ for arbitrarily large $x$, then $\int_x^{\lambda x} \frac{\theta(t) - t}{t^2}\,dt \ge \int_1^\lambda \frac{\lambda - t}{t^2}\,dt > 0$ for those $x$, against convergence; $\lambda < 1$ is similar. Then $\theta(x) \le \pi(x)\log x$ and $\theta(x) \ge (1 - \varepsilon)\log x\,(\pi(x) - x^{1-\varepsilon})$ give $\pi(x) \log x / x \to 1$.

concepts.c:prime-number: The theorem counts primes up to $x$.
concepts.c:asymptotic: The claim is an asymptotic equivalence, a limit of a ratio.
concepts.c:logarithm: The density of primes near $x$ is about $1/\log x$.
concepts.c:riemann-zeta-function: Zeros of zeta on the line $\operatorname{Re} s = 1$ would block the proof.
concepts.c:chebyshev-function: The weighted count $\theta(x)$ is easier to control than $\pi(x)$.
concepts.c:laplace-transform: Newman's theorem turns analytic continuation of a Laplace transform into convergence.

source.ref: D. Zagier, Newman's short proof of the prime number theorem, The American Mathematical Monthly 104 (1997), no. 8, 705-708
source.note: Zagier's account of D. J. Newman's 1980 proof; the steps follow its parts (I) to (VI) and its analytic theorem.

statement: Let $X = U \cup V$ be an [open cover](c:open-cover) by [path-connected](c:path-connected-space) sets with $U \cap V$ path-connected and $x_0 \in U \cap V$. Then the map $\Phi$ induced by the inclusions from the [free product](c:free-product) $\pi_1(U) * \pi_1(V)$ to $\pi_1(X)$ is surjective with kernel the [normal subgroup](c:normal-subgroup) $N$ generated by $i_U(\omega)\, i_V(\omega)^{-1}$, $\omega \in \pi_1(U \cap V)$.

hypotheses.text: The sets $U$ and $V$ are open in $X$ and $X = U \cup V$.
The sets $U$ and $V$ are [path-connected](c:path-connected-space).
The intersection $U \cap V$ is path-connected and contains the base point $x_0$.

conclusion: The [fundamental group](c:fundamental-group) $\pi_1(X, x_0)$ is the [amalgamated free product](c:amalgamated-product) $\pi_1(U) *_{\pi_1(U \cap V)} \pi_1(V)$.

proofs.name: Subdivision of loops and homotopies
proofs.slogan: Subdivide loops and homotopies into pieces that lie in $U$ or in $V$, and track how the factorizations change from piece to piece.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem for two open sets, as a case of Hatcher's proof for covers with path-connected double and triple intersections.

roles.why: Openness makes the preimages of $U$ and $V$ an [open cover](c:open-cover) of $I$ and of $I \times I$.
Path-connectedness of $U$ and of $V$ joins a grid vertex that lies in one set only to $x_0$ inside that set.
Path-connectedness of $U \cap V$ joins division points and grid vertices in both sets to $x_0$ inside $U \cap V$.

steps.slogan: Subdivide a loop at $x_0$ into paths that each lie in $U$ or in $V$.
steps.detail: For a loop $f$, the preimages of $U$ and $V$ form an [open cover](c:open-cover) of the compact interval $[0, 1]$. The Lebesgue number lemma gives $0 = s_0 < \dots < s_m = 1$ with each $f([s_{k-1}, s_k])$ in $U$ or in $V$; merging neighbors in the same set puts each $f(s_k)$, $0 < k < m$, in $U \cap V$.

steps.slogan: Join each division point to $x_0$ inside $U \cap V$ to prove that $\Phi$ is surjective.
steps.detail: Choose paths $g_k$ in $U \cap V$ from $x_0$ to $f(s_k)$, and let $f_k$ be the restriction of $f$ to $[s_{k-1}, s_k]$. Then $[f] = [f_1 \bar g_1][g_1 f_2 \bar g_2] \cdots [g_{m-1} f_m]$, and each factor is a loop at $x_0$ in $U$ or in $V$.

steps.slogan: Check that the [normal subgroup](c:normal-subgroup) $N$ lies in the kernel of $\Phi$.
steps.detail: For a loop $\omega$ in $U \cap V$, the classes $i_U(\omega)$ and $i_V(\omega)$ have the same image in $\pi_1(X)$. So $\Phi(i_U(\omega) i_V(\omega)^{-1}) = 1$, and the kernel is normal, so it contains $N$.

steps.slogan: Cut a homotopy between two factorizations into small rectangles that map into $U$ or $V$.
steps.detail: If two words of the [free product](c:free-product) have the same image, a homotopy $F\colon I \times I \to X$ joins the two products of loops. The Lebesgue number lemma gives a grid of rectangles that $F$ maps into $U$ or $V$; shift the grid so each vertex meets at most three rectangles, and join each vertex image to $x_0$ inside the sets of its rectangles.

steps.slogan: Show that crossing one rectangle changes the word only by an element of $N$.
steps.detail: Pushing the path across one rectangle replaces a factor by a homotopic loop in the same open set, or regards a loop in $U \cap V$ as a loop in $U$ instead of $V$. These moves change the word by elements of $N$, so every element of $\ker \Phi$ lies in $N$.

steps.slogan: Pass to the quotient by $N$ to obtain the isomorphism.
steps.detail: Steps 2, 3 and 5 show that $\Phi$ is surjective with kernel $N$. The first isomorphism theorem gives $(\pi_1(U) * \pi_1(V))/N \cong \pi_1(X, x_0)$, and the left side is the [amalgamated free product](c:amalgamated-product) by definition.

concepts.c:open-cover: Open sets let the Lebesgue number lemma subdivide loops and homotopies.
concepts.c:path-connected-space: Path-connectedness lets every subdivision point be joined to the base point.
concepts.c:free-product: Words in the free product record a loop as a product of pieces.
concepts.c:normal-subgroup: The relations from loops in $U \cap V$ generate the kernel as a normal subgroup.
concepts.c:fundamental-group: The theorem computes the fundamental group of $X$ from its pieces.
concepts.c:amalgamated-product: The quotient of the free product by $N$ is the amalgamated product.

source.note: A. Hatcher, Algebraic Topology, Theorem 1.20 and its proof.

statement: Let $E$ be a [separable](c:separable-space) [normed space](c:normed-space) over $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$. Then every closed [ball](c:ball) of the [dual space](c:dual-space) $E^*$ is sequentially compact in the [weak-* topology](c:weak-topology-2): every sequence in the ball has a subsequence $(\varphi_{k_j})$ with $\varphi_{k_j}(x) \to \varphi(x)$ for all $x \in E$, for some $\varphi$ in the ball.

hypotheses.text: The normed space $E$ is [separable](c:separable-space): it has a countable dense subset.
The sequence $(\varphi_k)$ lies in a closed ball $\{\varphi \in E^* : \|\varphi - \varphi_0\| \le r\}$ of the dual.

conclusion: Some subsequence of $(\varphi_k)$ converges in the weak-* topology to a functional $\varphi$ with $\|\varphi - \varphi_0\| \le r$.

formal.difference: The declaration is more general: the scalars may be any proper nontrivially normed field and $E$ may be seminormed.

proofs.name: Compact and metrizable
proofs.slogan: The ball is weak-* compact by Banach–Alaoglu, separability makes it metrizable, and a compact metrizable space is sequentially compact.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem for $r \ge 0$; for $r < 0$ the ball is empty and the claim is vacuous.

roles.why: Separability supplies the countable dense sequence that defines the metric.
The ball is bounded and weak-* closed, which the Banach–Alaoglu theorem needs.

steps.slogan: Show that the closed ball is weak-* compact by the Banach–Alaoglu theorem.
steps.detail: The ball is norm bounded, and it is weak-* closed as the intersection of the weak-* closed sets $\{\varphi : |\varphi(x) - \varphi_0(x)| \le r\|x\|\}$. The Banach–Alaoglu theorem makes bounded weak-* closed sets of $E^*$ compact in the [weak-* topology](c:weak-topology-2).

steps.slogan: Separate the points of the dual by evaluations at a dense sequence.
steps.detail: Let $(x_n)$ be a [dense](c:dense-set) sequence in $E$. The maps $\varphi \mapsto \varphi(x_n)$ are weak-* continuous, and if $\varphi(x_n) = \psi(x_n)$ for all $n$, then $\varphi = \psi$ by continuity and density.

steps.slogan: Build a metric for the weak-* topology on the compact ball.
steps.detail: Set $d(\varphi, \psi) = \sum_n 2^{-n} \min(1, |\varphi(x_n) - \psi(x_n)|)$, a metric by step 2 whose topology is weaker than the weak-* topology. The identity from the compact ball to the Hausdorff space $(\text{ball}, d)$ is a continuous bijection, hence a homeomorphism, so the ball is [metrizable](c:metrizable-space).

steps.slogan: Extract a convergent subsequence in the compact metric ball.
steps.detail: A compact metric space is [sequentially compact](c:seq-compact-space), so every sequence in the ball has a subsequence that converges in $d$, hence in the weak-* topology, to a point of the ball.

concepts.c:separable-space: A countable dense set gives countably many coordinates for a metric.
concepts.c:normed-space: The dual of a normed space carries the operator norm and its balls.
concepts.c:ball: Closed balls are the bounded weak-* closed sets that become compact.
concepts.c:dual-space: The compact set lives in the dual space $E^*$.
concepts.c:weak-topology-2: Compactness holds for the weak-* topology, not for the norm topology.
concepts.c:dense-set: Evaluations at a dense sequence already separate functionals.
concepts.c:metrizable-space: Metrizability turns compactness into sequential compactness.
concepts.c:seq-compact-space: Sequential compactness is the conclusion of the theorem.

proofs.name: Diagonal subsequence
proofs.slogan: Make the sequence converge at each point of a dense sequence by a diagonal argument, then extend the convergence to all of $E$ by the uniform bound.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem; $M = \|\varphi_0\| + r$ bounds every $\|\varphi_k\|$.

roles.why: Separability gives the countable dense sequence for the diagonal argument.
The uniform bound $M$ gives bounded scalar sequences, controls the error term and puts the limit in the ball.

steps.slogan: Choose nested subsequences that converge at $x_1, x_2, \dots$ and take the diagonal.
steps.detail: Let $(x_n)$ be a [dense](c:dense-set) sequence in $E$. The scalars $\varphi_k(x_n)$ satisfy $|\varphi_k(x_n)| \le M\|x_n\|$, so the Bolzano–Weierstrass theorem gives nested subsequences converging at $x_1$, then at $x_2$, and so on; the diagonal subsequence $(\psi_j)$ converges at every $x_n$.

steps.slogan: Show that $\psi_j(x)$ is a Cauchy sequence for every $x \in E$.
steps.detail: Given $x$ and $\varepsilon > 0$, pick $x_n$ with $\|x - x_n\| < \varepsilon$. Then $|\psi_j(x) - \psi_l(x)| \le 2M\varepsilon + |\psi_j(x_n) - \psi_l(x_n)|$, which is below $(2M+1)\varepsilon$ for large $j$ and $l$.

steps.slogan: Define the limit functional and check that it lies in the ball.
steps.detail: Set $\varphi(x) = \lim_j \psi_j(x)$; it is linear as a pointwise limit of linear maps. Also $|\varphi(x) - \varphi_0(x)| = \lim_j |\psi_j(x) - \varphi_0(x)| \le r\|x\|$, so $\varphi$ lies in the closed [ball](c:ball) of $E^*$ and $\psi_j \to \varphi$ in the weak-* topology.

concepts.c:separable-space: Separability makes a diagonal argument over countably many points possible.
concepts.c:normed-space: The norm of $E$ controls the error $|\psi_j(x) - \psi_j(x_n)|$.
concepts.c:ball: The closed ball bound passes to the pointwise limit.
concepts.c:dual-space: The limit is again a bounded linear functional in $E^*$.
concepts.c:weak-topology-2: Pointwise convergence on $E$ is convergence in the weak-* topology.
concepts.c:dense-set: Convergence on a dense sequence extends to all of $E$.

source.note: The classical diagonal argument with a three-epsilon extension from a dense sequence; not the mathlib route.

statement: Let $X_n$ and $Y_n$ be [random variables](c:random-variable) on one probability space with values in separable normed spaces, with $X_n \to X$ [in distribution](c:convergence-in-distribution) and $Y_n \to c$ [in probability](c:convergence-in-probability) for a constant $c$. Then $(X_n, Y_n) \to (X, c)$ in distribution, so $g(X_n, Y_n) \to g(X, c)$ for every [continuous](c:continuous-function) $g$; in particular $X_n + Y_n \to X + c$.

hypotheses.text: The sequence $X_n$ converges to $X$ [in distribution](c:convergence-in-distribution).
Each $Y_n$ lives on the probability space of $X_n$, and $Y_n \to c$ [in probability](c:convergence-in-probability) for a constant $c$.
The map $g$ is [continuous](c:continuous-function) on the product of the two value spaces.

formal.difference: The declaration works along any countably generated filter and lets the limit $X$ live on another probability space; the value spaces are second countable seminormed groups.

proofs.name: Converging together and continuous mapping
proofs.slogan: Show that $(X_n, c) \to (X, c)$, that $(X_n, Y_n)$ stays close to it in probability, and apply the continuous mapping theorem.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem; the classical cases take $g(x, y) = x + y$ and $g(x, y) = yx$.

roles.why: Convergence of $X_n$ gives the limit of the comparison pair $(X_n, c)$.
Convergence of $Y_n$ to a constant makes the two pairs close in probability; the common space makes the pair defined.
Continuity of $g$ lets the continuous mapping theorem carry the limit through $g$.

steps.slogan: Push $X_n \to X$ forward along the continuous map $x \mapsto (x, c)$.
steps.detail: The map $x \mapsto (x, c)$ is [continuous](c:continuous-function), so the continuous mapping theorem gives $(X_n, c) \to (X, c)$ in distribution.

steps.slogan: Show that the distance between $(X_n, Y_n)$ and $(X_n, c)$ tends to zero in probability.
steps.detail: The distance is $\|(0, Y_n - c)\| = \|Y_n - c\|$, and $P(\|Y_n - c\| \ge \varepsilon) \to 0$ for every $\varepsilon > 0$ because $Y_n \to c$ [in probability](c:convergence-in-probability).

steps.slogan: Show that pairs close in probability share the limit in distribution, using bounded Lipschitz test functions.
steps.detail: For $F$ with oscillation at most $M$ and [Lipschitz](c:lipschitz-function) constant $L$, $|E F(X_n, Y_n) - E F(X_n, c)| \le L\varepsilon + M\,P(\|Y_n - c\| \ge \varepsilon)$. With steps 1 and 2, $E F(X_n, Y_n) \to E F(X, c)$, and bounded Lipschitz functions determine convergence in distribution, so $(X_n, Y_n) \to (X, c)$.

steps.slogan: Apply the continuous mapping theorem to $g$ and the convergent pair.
steps.detail: Since $g$ is continuous and $(X_n, Y_n) \to (X, c)$ [in distribution](c:convergence-in-distribution), the continuous mapping theorem gives $g(X_n, Y_n) \to g(X, c)$ in distribution.

concepts.c:random-variable: The theorem combines two sequences of random variables on one space.
concepts.c:convergence-in-distribution: Convergence in distribution is the mode of the hypothesis and the conclusion.
concepts.c:convergence-in-probability: Convergence in probability to a constant keeps the pair close to $(X_n, c)$.
concepts.c:continuous-function: Continuous maps preserve convergence in distribution.
concepts.c:lipschitz-function: Lipschitz test functions turn small distances into small changes of expectations.

statement: For every $\varepsilon > 0$ and integer $l \ge 1$ there is $M(\varepsilon, l)$ such that every finite [graph](c:graph) with at least $l$ vertices has an equipartition (a [partition](c:finpartition) with part sizes differing by at most one) into $k$ parts, $l \le k \le M(\varepsilon, l)$, in which at most $\varepsilon k(k-1)$ ordered pairs of distinct parts fail to be $\varepsilon$-regular.

hypotheses.text: The parameter satisfies $\varepsilon > 0$.
The graph $G$ is a finite simple [graph](c:graph) on $n$ vertices.
The graph has at least $l$ vertices: $n \ge l$.

conclusion: There is an equipartition into $k$ parts, $l \le k \le M(\varepsilon, l)$, in which all but $\varepsilon k(k-1)$ ordered pairs $(A, B)$ of distinct parts satisfy $|d(A', B') - d(A, B)| < \varepsilon$ for all $A' \subseteq A$ and $B' \subseteq B$ with $|A'| \ge \varepsilon |A|$ and $|B'| \ge \varepsilon |B|$, where $d$ is the [edge density](c:edge-density).

formal.difference: The declaration gives the explicit bound SzemerediRegularity.bound ε l for $M(\varepsilon, l)$.

proofs.name: Energy increment
proofs.slogan: Refine a non-regular equipartition so that its energy rises by $\varepsilon^5/4$; since the energy stays at most $1$, the refinement stops after at most $4/\varepsilon^5$ rounds.
proofs.scope: The whole lemma; step 1 treats graphs with at most $M$ vertices. For $\varepsilon \ge 1$ every equipartition works, so steps 2 to 5 assume $\varepsilon < 1$.

roles.why: A positive $\varepsilon$ makes the energy gain $\varepsilon^5/4$ positive, so the number of rounds is finite.
A finite graph has edge densities in $[0, 1]$, so the energy is defined and bounded by $1$.
At least $l$ vertices allow the singleton partition or a starting equipartition with $t \ge l$ parts.

steps.slogan: Take the partition into singletons when the graph has at most $M$ vertices.
steps.detail: If $l \le n \le M$, the singletons form an equipartition with $n$ parts. Two singletons always form an $\varepsilon$-regular pair, because a subset of a singleton with at least $\varepsilon$ elements is the singleton itself.

steps.slogan: Start from an arbitrary equipartition with $t$ parts for a fixed large $t \ge l$.
steps.detail: For $n > M$, choose an equipartition into $t = t(\varepsilon, l)$ parts with $t \ge l$ and $4^t \varepsilon^5 \ge 100$. The constant $M$ is fixed in step 5 so that $n$ is large enough for every later refinement.

steps.slogan: Define the energy of a partition and bound it by one.
steps.detail: For parts $V_1, \dots, V_k$, set $q = k^{-2} \sum_{i \ne j} d(V_i, V_j)^2$. Every [edge density](c:edge-density) lies in $[0, 1]$, so $0 \le q \le 1$.

steps.slogan: Refine each part by the witness sets of its irregular pairs to raise the energy by $\varepsilon^5/4$.
steps.detail: If more than $\varepsilon k(k-1)$ pairs are irregular, cut each part by the witness sets $A', B'$ of its irregular pairs and re-cut into an equipartition with at most $k\,4^k$ parts. The defect form of the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality shows that each irregular pair adds about $\varepsilon^4$ to its share of the energy, so $q$ rises by at least $\varepsilon^5/4$.

steps.slogan: Stop after at most $4/\varepsilon^5$ increments and bound the final number of parts.
steps.detail: Since $q \le 1$ and each round adds $\varepsilon^5/4$, an $\varepsilon$-regular equipartition appears within $4/\varepsilon^5$ rounds. The number of parts stays between $t \ge l$ and the $(\lfloor 4/\varepsilon^5 \rfloor + 1)$-fold iterate of $k \mapsto k\,4^k$ at $t$, which with a margin for the re-cuts defines $M(\varepsilon, l)$.

concepts.c:graph: The lemma partitions the vertex set of any finite graph.
concepts.c:finpartition: The proof refines finite partitions of the vertex set step by step.
concepts.c:edge-density: Regularity and energy are both defined through edge densities.

statement: Let $(X_i)_{i \in I}$ be any family of [compact](c:compact-space) topological spaces. Then the product $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ with the [product topology](c:product-topology) is compact.

hypotheses.text: Every factor $X_i$ is [compact](c:compact-space).

conclusion: The product space $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is compact.

formal.difference: The declaration states it for compact subsets $s_i \subseteq X_i$: the set of $x$ with $x_i \in s_i$ for all $i$ is compact. The case $s_i = X_i$ is this theorem.

proofs.name: Ultrafilter limits
proofs.slogan: An [ultrafilter](c:ultrafilter) on the product projects to an ultrafilter on each factor, each projection converges, and the chosen limits form a limit of the ultrafilter.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, with the axiom of choice, which Tychonoff's theorem implies. An empty factor makes the product empty, and the empty space is compact.

roles.why: Compactness of each factor makes each projected ultrafilter converge.

steps.slogan: Characterize compactness by convergence of every ultrafilter.
steps.detail: A space is compact if and only if every ultrafilter on it converges. If an open cover has no finite subcover, the complements of the finite unions generate a [filter](c:filter), and the ultrafilter lemma extends it to an ultrafilter that converges nowhere.

steps.slogan: Push an ultrafilter $\mathcal U$ on the product forward along each projection $p_i$.
steps.detail: The image $p_i(\mathcal U) = \{A \subseteq X_i : p_i^{-1}(A) \in \mathcal U\}$ is an ultrafilter on $X_i$, because taking preimages under $p_i$ preserves complements and intersections.

steps.slogan: Choose a limit $x_i$ of each projected ultrafilter in its compact factor.
steps.detail: Each $X_i$ is [compact](c:compact-space), so $p_i(\mathcal U)$ converges to some $x_i \in X_i$ by step 1. The [axiom of choice](c:axiom-of-choice) picks one limit for every $i$ at once and gives the point $x = (x_i)_{i \in I}$.

steps.slogan: Show that $\mathcal U$ converges to $x$ in the product topology.
steps.detail: A basic neighborhood of $x$ in the [product topology](c:product-topology) is $\bigcap_{i \in F} p_i^{-1}(W_i)$ with $F$ finite and $W_i$ open around $x_i$. Each $p_i^{-1}(W_i)$ lies in $\mathcal U$ because $p_i(\mathcal U) \to x_i$, so the finite intersection lies in $\mathcal U$, and the product is compact by step 1.

concepts.c:compact-space: Compactness of the factors gives limits of the projected ultrafilters.
concepts.c:product-topology: Convergence in the product topology is convergence in each coordinate.
concepts.c:ultrafilter: Ultrafilters converge in compact spaces and project to ultrafilters.
concepts.c:filter: A cover without finite subcover yields a filter that extends to an ultrafilter.
concepts.c:axiom-of-choice: Choice selects one limit in each of the possibly infinitely many factors.

proofs.name: Alexander's subbase theorem
proofs.slogan: By Alexander's subbase theorem, test only covers by cylinder sets $p_i^{-1}(U)$, and find a point outside any such cover without a finite subcover.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. Alexander's theorem uses Zorn's lemma, and the choice of one uncovered point in each factor uses the axiom of choice.

roles.why: Compactness of the factor $X_i$ turns a cover of $X_i$ from $\mathcal C_i$ into a finite one.

steps.slogan: Reduce to covers by subbasic cylinder sets with Alexander's subbase theorem.
steps.detail: The sets $p_i^{-1}(U)$ with $U \subseteq X_i$ open form a subbase of the [product topology](c:product-topology). Alexander's subbase theorem says that a space is compact when every cover by subbasic sets has a finite subcover.

steps.slogan: Find in each factor a point that the cover sets of that factor miss.
steps.detail: Let $\mathcal C$ be a cover by cylinders with no finite subcover, and let $\mathcal C_i = \{U : p_i^{-1}(U) \in \mathcal C\}$. If $\mathcal C_i$ covered the [compact](c:compact-space) $X_i$, finitely many of its sets would cover $X_i$, and their cylinders would cover the product. So some $x_i \in X_i$ lies in no member of $\mathcal C_i$.

steps.slogan: Assemble the uncovered coordinates into a point that no cylinder of the cover contains.
steps.detail: The [axiom of choice](c:axiom-of-choice) picks $x_i$ for every $i$ and gives $x = (x_i)$. If $x \in p_i^{-1}(U) \in \mathcal C$, then $x_i \in U \in \mathcal C_i$, against the choice of $x_i$; so $\mathcal C$ is not a cover, a contradiction, and the product is compact.

concepts.c:compact-space: Compactness of one factor gives the finite subcover that leads to the contradiction.
concepts.c:product-topology: The cylinder sets form a subbase of the product topology.
concepts.c:axiom-of-choice: Choice assembles one uncovered coordinate from every factor.

statement: Let $(X, \mu)$ be a measure space, $1 \le p < \infty$, and $f_n, g$ in the [Lp space](c:lp-space) $L^p(\mu)$. Then $\|f_n - g\|_p \to 0$ if and only if $f_n \to g$ [in measure](c:convergence-in-measure), $(f_n)$ is [uniformly integrable](c:uniform-integrability) (sets of small measure carry uniformly small $p$-norm) and uniformly tight (some set of finite measure carries all but a uniformly small $p$-norm).

hypotheses.text: The exponent satisfies $1 \le p < \infty$.
The functions $f_n$ and $g$ lie in the [Lp space](c:lp-space) $L^p(\mu)$.

conclusion: $f_n \to g$ in $L^p$ exactly when $f_n \to g$ in measure and $(f_n)$ is uniformly integrable and uniformly tight.

proofs.name: Subsequences, Egorov and Markov
proofs.slogan: Forward, pass to almost everywhere convergent subsequences, cut off a finite-measure set by tightness and use Egorov with uniform integrability; backward, use Markov's inequality and the $L^p$ error.
proofs.scope: Both directions; for $\mu = 0$ everything is trivial. Steps 1 to 4 prove the forward direction, and steps 5 and 6 the converse.

roles.why: For $p \ge 1$ the $p$-norm obeys Minkowski's inequality, and $p < \infty$ lets Markov's inequality and small sets control it.
Each single function of $L^p$, such as $g$, is uniformly integrable and tight.

steps.slogan: Reduce the forward direction to almost everywhere convergence by passing to subsequences.
steps.detail: A real sequence tends to $0$ if every subsequence has a further subsequence tending to $0$. Every subsequence of $(f_n)$ still converges [in measure](c:convergence-in-measure), so it has a further subsequence converging to $g$ [almost everywhere](c:almost-everywhere), and it keeps uniform integrability and tightness.

steps.slogan: Cut off a set $E$ of finite measure by uniform tightness.
steps.detail: Given $\varepsilon > 0$, tightness of $(f_n)$ and of the single function $g$ gives $E$ with $\mu(E) < \infty$, $\|f_n 1_{E^c}\|_p \le \varepsilon$ for all $n$ and $\|g 1_{E^c}\|_p \le \varepsilon$.

steps.slogan: Apply Egorov's theorem on $E$ to get uniform convergence off a small set.
steps.detail: [Uniform integrability](c:uniform-integrability) of $(f_n)$ and of $g$ gives $\delta > 0$ with $\|f_n 1_A\|_p \le \varepsilon$ and $\|g 1_A\|_p \le \varepsilon$ when $\mu(A) \le \delta$. Egorov's theorem on the finite measure set $E$ gives $B \subseteq E$ with $\mu(B) \le \delta$ and $f_n \to g$ [uniformly](c:uniform-convergence) on $E \setminus B$.

steps.slogan: Add the three pieces with Minkowski's inequality to bound $\|f_n - g\|_p$.
steps.detail: Splitting over $E \setminus B$, $B$ and $E^c$, Minkowski's inequality gives $\|f_n - g\|_p \le \mu(E)^{1/p} \sup_{E \setminus B} |f_n - g| + 2\varepsilon + 2\varepsilon$. The first term tends to $0$, so $\limsup_n \|f_n - g\|_p \le 4\varepsilon$ along the subsequence.

steps.slogan: Derive convergence in measure from $L^p$ convergence by Markov's inequality.
steps.detail: For $\eta > 0$, Markov's inequality applied to $|f_n - g|^p$ gives $\mu(|f_n - g| \ge \eta) \le \eta^{-p} \|f_n - g\|_p^p$, which tends to $0$.

steps.slogan: Transfer uniform integrability and tightness from finitely many functions and $g$ to the sequence.
steps.detail: Choose $N$ with $\|f_n - g\|_p \le \varepsilon$ for $n > N$; then $\|f_n 1_A\|_p \le \|g 1_A\|_p + \varepsilon$. Dominated convergence makes each single function of $L^p$ uniformly integrable and tight, so $g, f_1, \dots, f_N$ give one $\delta$ and one set $E$ that work for every $n$.

steps.slogan: Join the two directions into the stated equivalence.
steps.detail: Steps 1 to 4 show that convergence in measure, uniform integrability and uniform tightness give $\|f_n - g\|_p \to 0$. Steps 5 and 6 show that $L^p$ convergence gives the three properties.

concepts.c:lp-space: The theorem characterizes convergence in the norm of $L^p$.
concepts.c:convergence-in-measure: Convergence in measure gives almost everywhere convergent subsequences.
concepts.c:uniform-integrability: Uniform integrability controls the norm on the small exceptional set.
concepts.c:almost-everywhere: Egorov's theorem needs almost everywhere convergence on $E$.
concepts.c:uniform-convergence: Uniform convergence off a small set bounds the main piece.

statement: Let $(f_n)$ be a submartingale, a [martingale](c:martingale) up to $E[f_{n+1} \mid \mathcal F_n] \ge f_n$, for a [filtration](c:filtration) $(\mathcal F_n)$ on a finite measure space, with $\|f_n\|_1 \le R$ for all $n$. Then $f_n$ converges [almost everywhere](c:almost-everywhere) to a real-valued function that is measurable for $\mathcal F_\infty = \bigvee_n \mathcal F_n$.

hypotheses.text: The measure $\mu$ is finite.
The process $(f_n)$ is adapted to the [filtration](c:filtration) $(\mathcal F_n)$, integrable, and satisfies $E[f_{n+1} \mid \mathcal F_n] \ge f_n$.
The process is bounded in $L^1$: $\|f_n\|_1 \le R$ for all $n$.

conclusion: There is an $\mathcal F_\infty$-measurable $f_\infty\colon \Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ with $f_n \to f_\infty$ almost everywhere.

proofs.name: Upcrossings and Fatou
proofs.slogan: Doob's upcrossing estimate makes the upcrossings of every rational interval finite almost everywhere, and Fatou's lemma rules out infinite limits.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem; the limit is set to $0$ on the null set where the sequence has no finite limit.

roles.why: A finite measure makes $E[(f_N - a)^+] \le R + |a|\,\mu(\Omega)$ finite.
The submartingale property drives Doob's upcrossing estimate, and adaptedness makes the limit $\mathcal F_\infty$-measurable.
The $L^1$ bound makes the upcrossing bound uniform in $N$ and Fatou's bound finite.

steps.slogan: Bound the expected number of upcrossings of $[a, b]$ by Doob's upcrossing estimate.
steps.detail: Let $U_N(a, b)$ count the upcrossings of $[a, b]$ by $f_0, \dots, f_N$. Doob's estimate for the submartingale gives $(b - a)\, E[U_N(a, b)] \le E[(f_N - a)^+] \le R + |a|\,\mu(\Omega)$ for every $N$.

steps.slogan: Show that all rational intervals have finitely many upcrossings outside one null set.
steps.detail: Monotone convergence gives $E[U_\infty(a, b)] \le (R + |a|\,\mu(\Omega))/(b - a) < \infty$, so $U_\infty(a, b) < \infty$ [almost everywhere](c:almost-everywhere). The union of the exceptional null sets over the countably many rational pairs $a < b$ is still null.

steps.slogan: Exclude oscillation, because finite upcrossings force $\liminf f_n = \limsup f_n$.
steps.detail: If $\liminf_n f_n(\omega) < a < b < \limsup_n f_n(\omega)$ for rationals $a, b$, the sequence crosses $[a, b]$ upward infinitely often. So outside the null set of step 2, $f_n(\omega)$ has a limit in $[-\infty, \infty]$.

steps.slogan: Bound $\liminf |f_n|$ by Fatou's lemma to exclude infinite limits.
steps.detail: Fatou's lemma gives $E[\liminf_n |f_n|] \le \liminf_n E|f_n| \le R$, so $\liminf_n |f_n| < \infty$ almost everywhere. Hence a limit in $[-\infty, \infty]$ is finite almost everywhere.

steps.slogan: Define the limit function and check that it is $\mathcal F_\infty$-measurable.
steps.detail: Set $f_\infty = \lim_n f_n$ where a finite limit exists and $f_\infty = 0$ elsewhere; by steps 3 and 4, $f_n \to f_\infty$ almost everywhere. Each $f_n$ is $\mathcal F_n$-measurable for the [filtration](c:filtration), hence $\mathcal F_\infty$-measurable, so the convergence set and $f_\infty$ are $\mathcal F_\infty$-measurable.

concepts.c:martingale: The submartingale inequality is what the upcrossing estimate needs.
concepts.c:filtration: The limit is measurable for the sigma-algebra generated by the filtration.
concepts.c:almost-everywhere: The convergence holds outside a countable union of null sets.

statement: Let $D\colon \Gamma(E) \to \Gamma(F)$ be an [elliptic](c:elliptic-operator) differential operator between smooth complex [vector bundles](c:vector-bundle) over a closed [compact manifold](c:compact-manifold) $M$. Then $D$ is Fredholm, and its analytical [index](c:fredholm-index) $\dim \ker D - \dim \operatorname{coker} D$ equals its topological index, computed from the symbol class in the [K-theory](c:topological-k-theory) of $T^*M$ or, by the cohomological formula, from [characteristic classes](c:characteristic-class).

hypotheses.text: The manifold $M$ is smooth, [compact](c:compact-manifold) and without boundary.
The operator $D$ is a linear differential operator whose principal symbol $\sigma(D)(x, \xi)\colon E_x \to F_x$ is invertible for every nonzero covector $\xi$.

conclusion: $\operatorname{ind}_a(D) = \operatorname{ind}_t(D)$, where $\operatorname{ind}_t(D)$ is the image of $[\sigma(D)] \in K_c(T^*M)$ under the topological pushforward $K_c(T^*M) \to K_c(T^*\mathrm{pt}) = \mathbb{Z}$.

proofs.name: K-theory embedding proof
proofs.slogan: Show that both indices are homomorphisms on $K_c(T^*M)$ that obey the same excision and Thom axioms, and that these axioms force equality with the topological index.
proofs.scope: An outline of the second proof of Atiyah and Singer; every step rests on the cited paper. The cohomological formula follows later from the Chern character (Index III).

roles.why: Compactness makes the parametrix errors compact operators and allows an embedding of $M$ in $\mathbb{R}^N$.
An invertible symbol off the zero section gives a parametrix and a class in $K_c(T^*M)$.

steps.slogan: Build a parametrix for $D$ to show that $D$ is Fredholm.
steps.detail: Ellipticity lets one invert the symbol and build a [pseudodifferential operator](c:pseudodifferential-operator) $Q$ with $QD - 1$ and $DQ - 1$ of order $-1$. On Sobolev spaces of the compact manifold these errors are compact by Rellich's lemma, so $D$ is Fredholm.

steps.slogan: Show that the analytical index depends only on the symbol class in $K_c(T^*M)$.
steps.detail: The Fredholm index is constant under norm-continuous deformations, and elliptic pseudodifferential operators with homotopic symbols deform into each other. So the analytical index defines a homomorphism $\operatorname{ind}_a\colon K_c(T^*M) \to \mathbb{Z}$.

steps.slogan: Prove that the analytical index respects open embeddings and the Thom isomorphism.
steps.detail: For an open embedding of manifolds, the index of an operator trivial at infinity does not depend on the ambient manifold (excision). For an embedding with normal bundle $N$, the index is compatible with the [Thom isomorphism](c:thom-isomorphism) $K_c(T^*M) \to K_c(T^*N)$, by Bott periodicity on the fibres and a multiplicative property.

steps.slogan: Define the topological index by embedding $M$ in $\mathbb{R}^N$ and pushing the symbol to a point.
steps.detail: Embed $M$ in $\mathbb{R}^N$, map $K_c(T^*M)$ by the Thom isomorphism to the tubular neighborhood, extend by zero to $K_c(T^*\mathbb{R}^N)$, and use Bott periodicity $K_c(T^*\mathbb{R}^N) \cong \mathbb{Z}$. The result does not depend on the embedding.

steps.slogan: Show that the axioms force the analytical index to equal the topological index.
steps.detail: Both indices satisfy the excision and Thom axioms and agree on a point, where both are the identity of $\mathbb{Z}$. Running the definition of $\operatorname{ind}_t$ through these axioms gives $\operatorname{ind}_a = \operatorname{ind}_t$ on all of $K_c(T^*M)$.

concepts.c:elliptic-operator: Ellipticity makes the operator Fredholm and its symbol a K-theory class.
concepts.c:vector-bundle: The operator acts on sections of vector bundles over $M$.
concepts.c:compact-manifold: Compactness gives finite-dimensional kernel and cokernel.
concepts.c:fredholm-index: The analytical index is the Fredholm index of $D$.
concepts.c:topological-k-theory: Both indices are homomorphisms out of compactly supported K-theory of $T^*M$.
concepts.c:characteristic-class: The cohomological form of the topological index uses characteristic classes.
concepts.c:pseudodifferential-operator: Pseudodifferential operators give the parametrix and the needed deformations.
concepts.c:thom-isomorphism: Compatibility with the Thom isomorphism is the key axiom.

source.ref: M. F. Atiyah and I. M. Singer, The index of elliptic operators I, Annals of Mathematics 87 (1968), 484-530
